lead: Chrysin (5,7-dihydroxyflavone) is a flavone, a type of flavonoid, found in honey, propolis, passionflowers (Passiflora species), Scutellaria baicalensis and some mushrooms and fruits [2][3]. It is an ingredient in some dietary supplements [2].

In bodybuilding and hormone-management supplement culture it is sold as a natural estrogen blocker: the claim is that it inhibits aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, and so could raise or protect testosterone relative to estrogen. People who use it for this purpose are generally aiming for a leaner, drier, more muscular look and for fewer estrogen-related effects such as water retention and gynecomastia. Wikipedia states that oral chrysin has no clinical aromatase-inhibitor activity and that there is no evidence it affects testosterone levels [2]. Its oral bioavailability is reported as very low, between 0.003 and 0.02 percent [2].

A large preclinical literature describes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and neurological effects in cells and animals [4][13]. Human clinical data are minimal: chrysin has been an ingredient in multi-component hormone supplements tested in randomized trials [14][15], and two small studies of its bioavailability, safety and exercise physiology are registered [7][8]. Wikipedia's article on aromatase inhibitors describes the prescription drug class that chrysin is often compared to [28].

angle.text: Chrysin is marketed to people who want to limit estrogen conversion while training or while on testosterone therapy, in the hope of a drier, more muscular physique and less estrogenic side effects. The in-vitro aromatase activity of the molecule is the basis of this claim; clinical measurements have not reported an effect in humans.

infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement; FDA's compounding advisory committee did not recommend it for the 503A bulk list in 2016 [2]

sections.h: Background: estrogen, aromatase and the physique rationale
paras: Aromatase is the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into estrogens. Wikipedia's overview of aromatase inhibitors explains that drugs which block it are used mainly in hormone-sensitive breast cancer, and that off-label use in men to manage estrogen during testosterone therapy is also described [28]. Interest in an over-the-counter version grew in bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy circles, where estrogen is associated in popular discussion with water retention, a softer look and gynecomastia.

Chrysin became one of the best-known supplement candidates because flavones, the chemical family it belongs to, showed enzyme-blocking activity in test-tube assays [2][4]. The supplement pitch follows a three-step chain: oral chrysin blocks aromatase, less testosterone becomes estrogen, and the user ends up with a higher androgen-to-estrogen ratio and a leaner, harder look. Researchers who have followed that chain through to living people describe the middle step as the limiting one, because the compound reaches the bloodstream in very small amounts [2][9].

Chrysin has the formula C15H10O4, with hydroxyl groups at the 5 and 7 positions of a flavone skeleton [2][3]. It is a yellow crystalline solid with low water solubility [3]. It belongs to the B-ring unsubstituted flavones, a group whose pharmacokinetics were reviewed in 2019 [3].

Reported concentrations vary widely between sources. Wikipedia lists about 0.2 mg per 100 g in honey, 0.10 mg/kg in honeydew honey and 5.3 mg/kg in forest honeys in a 2010 study, with higher levels in propolis (a 2010 study reported up to 28 g/L), and 0.17 to 0.34 mg/kg in mushrooms from Lesvos [2]. Reviews of bee products in skin care and of propolis discuss chrysin as one of several flavonoids present [16][17].

Chrysin attracted attention because flavones inhibited aromatase in test-tube assays. Wikipedia cites a 2001 study by Saarinen and colleagues titled 'No evidence for the in vivo activity of aromatase-inhibiting flavonoids' and states that oral chrysin has no clinical aromatase-inhibitor activity [2]. In binding assays certain flavonoids and phytoestrogens interact with estrogen receptor beta [5].

Oral chrysin is poorly absorbed and rapidly excreted, with reported bioavailability of 0.003 to 0.02 percent [2]. A 2001 controlled study in volunteers examined its disposition and metabolism [9], and chrysin is conjugated to glucuronides and sulfates, as also described for propolis flavonoids [10]. Methylated flavonoids were reported in a 2006 study to have greatly improved intestinal absorption and metabolic stability compared with unmethylated ones [6]. Researchers are developing nanoformulations such as liposomes and nanocapsules to improve absorption [2].
Flavonoids as a class have been studied as inhibitors of the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 in vitro [18] and of the transporter ABCG2 [19].

Reviews describe chrysin's laboratory activities including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, neuroprotective and anxiolytic effects [4][13]. A 2022 cell study reported that chrysin sensitised osteosarcoma cells to TRAIL-induced apoptosis [20]. Wikipedia also lists chrysin among modulators of the xenobiotic-sensing receptor CAR [2].

In supplement catalogues chrysin appears alone and in blends marketed to men for testosterone support or as a so-called anti-aromatase. Hormone-focused products from the early 2000s paired it with androgen precursors, saw palmetto, indole-3-carbinol and tribulus, on the reasoning that it would limit conversion of the precursors to estrogens [14][15]. Practitioners and users of testosterone therapy have discussed chrysin in forums as a mild estrogen-management option; some doctors were reported by posters to use chrysin cream, a route for which Wikipedia notes there is no information on systemic exposure [2].

No published clinical studies isolate chrysin's effect on testosterone, estrogen or physique outcomes in men. Wikipedia states that as of 2016 there was no clinical use and no evidence that oral chrysin changes testosterone levels [2].

Two randomized trials from 2001 tested multi-ingredient supplements that contained chrysin. In one, 55 healthy men aged 30 to 59 received for 28 days either a product containing 300 mg androstenedione, 150 mg DHEA, saw palmetto, indole-3-carbinol, 625 mg chrysin and tribulus (n = 28) or placebo (n = 27), with the aim of raising testosterone while blocking formation of estrogens and DHT [14]. A companion trial gave men aged 30 to 58 a product with 300 mg androstenediol, saw palmetto, indole-3-carbinol, 300 mg chrysin, gamma-linolenic acid and tribulus (n = 28) or placebo, measuring endocrine and lipid responses [15]. A 2003 report from the same programme looked at immune function in middle-aged men taking a DHEA and androstenedione product [21]. Because chrysin was one of several active ingredients in each product, those trials cannot separate its contribution.

Two small studies are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov: an 18-person completed study of chrysin bioavailability and safety after oral intake, started in December 2024 [7], and a 15-person completed pilot of chrysin and exercise performance, started in January 2025 [8]. Results are not summarised on the registry entries.

Wikipedia reports that a 2017 review considers intake of 0.5 to 3 g per day safe, and that as of 2016 no toxicity had been attributed to chrysin in clinical trials or adverse event reports, though nonclinical data suggested possible concerns [2]. In 2016 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee did not recommend adding chrysin to the bulk drug substances list under section 503A, citing among other things insufficient information on its history of use in compounding [2].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Chrysin features in older bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy discussions. Posts on T Nation range from a 2001 reply stating that neither DIM nor chrysin had been shown to reduce estrogen levels in vivo [22], to a 2023 post suggesting DIM or chrysin as options to consider only after a stable testosterone protocol and lab work [23], to a 2019 comment recalling the time when chrysin 'was a thing for blocking estrogen' [24]. Supplement advertising of the mid-2000s also promoted high-strength chrysin products to older men [25].

Chrysin is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement, alone and inside multi-ingredient products marketed for testosterone support or as an anti-aromatase [14][15]. Supplement marketing of the early to mid 2000s promoted it directly to older men, and ads for high-strength chrysin products were discussed on bodybuilding forums at the time [25].

Forum conversation has shifted over two decades. Early threads on T Nation debated chrysin alongside other estrogen-modulating supplements and asked whether any had been shown to reduce estrogen in living people [22][26]. Later threads about testosterone therapy treat chrysin as a historical option, with posters recalling when it 'was a thing for blocking estrogen' [24] and others suggesting that lab work and a stable protocol come before any estrogen-management supplement [23].

Researchers have continued to study chrysin for other reasons. Reviews catalogue antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective and anticancer actions in cells and animals [4][13], and bee-product reviews list it among the flavonoids of propolis used in skin care and general health products [16][17].

Chrysin is one of several plant-derived compounds that bodybuilders and testosterone-therapy users discuss for estrogen management, including diindolylmethane and indole-3-carbinol, which appear alongside chrysin in the multi-ingredient products tested in the 2001 trials [14][15]. Wikipedia's aromatase-inhibitor article lists other foods and plants, including mushrooms, with reported aromatase-inhibiting activity in laboratory assays [28]. Prescription aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole are a separate, regulated drug class used for breast cancer and, off-label, by some men on testosterone therapy [28].

Current work centres on absorption. Methylated flavonoids showed much better intestinal absorption and metabolic stability than unmethylated ones in a 2006 study [6], and nanoformulations such as liposomes and nanocapsules are being developed to raise the amount of chrysin that reaches the blood [2]. Two small studies registered in 2024 and 2025 examine bioavailability and safety, and exercise performance [7][8].

lore.intro: Chrysin appears in bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy forums as an over-the-counter anti-estrogen alternative, with opinion ranging from enthusiasm in the early 2000s to scepticism in later threads [22][23][24].

claims.claim: Chrysin is a natural aromatase inhibitor that raises testosterone.
claims.believers: Supplement marketers and some users say that chrysin blocks aromatase in the way prescription inhibitors do, reducing estrogen conversion; a 2002 post on T Nation listed it among the 'most potent natural estrogen suppressors' alongside another supplement [26].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that oral chrysin has no clinical aromatase-inhibitor activity and no evidence of affecting testosterone [2]; reported oral bioavailability is very low [2].

claims.claim: Chrysin is a mild option for estrogen control on testosterone therapy.
claims.believers: Some forum users say that it is a gentle option to consider before stronger aromatase inhibitors once labs show high estradiol [23].
claims.experts: Other posters note it has not been shown to lower estrogen in vivo [22], consistent with Wikipedia's summary of the 2001 aromatase study [2].

claims.claim: Chrysin is safe at supplement doses.
claims.believers: Users generally describe it as very mild, and one poster characterised it as 'VERY mild' [27].
claims.experts: A 2017 review cited by Wikipedia considers 0.5 to 3 g daily safe and no toxicity had been attributed to it in trials or adverse event reports as of 2016, although nonclinical data suggested possible concerns [2].

claims.claim: Chrysin works better in combination with other anti-estrogen supplements.
claims.believers: Supplement makers of the early 2000s paired chrysin with androgen precursors, saw palmetto, indole-3-carbinol and tribulus, arguing the blend would shift hormones toward testosterone [14][15][26].
claims.experts: The two randomized trials of such blends each contained several active ingredients, so the contribution of chrysin cannot be separated from the rest [14][15].

claims.claim: Chrysin cream avoids the absorption problem of capsules.
claims.believers: Some posters on testosterone forums say that doctors in their area use chrysin cream as an estrogen-management option [23].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes there is no information on systemic exposure from topical chrysin [2].

claims.claim: Making chrysin more absorbable could unlock its aromatase effect.
claims.believers: Interest in methylated and nano-formulated flavonoids rests on the idea that the compound is active but poorly absorbed [6][2].
claims.experts: Methylated flavonoids were reported to be better absorbed in a 2006 study [6], and registered 2024 and 2025 studies are measuring chrysin bioavailability and exercise outcomes without published results on the registry [7][8].

name: Chrysin

card.summary: A passionflower and honey flavone sold as a weak aromatase inhibitor; poorly absorbed orally and no evidence it affects testosterone.
card.note: Oral bioavailability is reported as very low, and Wikipedia reports no evidence of clinical aromatase inhibition.

quick.overview:
Chrysin is a natural flavonoid found in honey, propolis and passionflower. In bodybuilding supplements it is promoted as a mild aromatase inhibitor, meaning something that would reduce conversion of testosterone to estrogen.

Laboratory studies have found a range of biological activities, but Wikipedia reports no evidence that oral chrysin has aromatase-inhibiting activity or affects testosterone in people. Registered human studies to date are small pilot studies of absorption, safety and exercise.
quick.mechanism: In cell and enzyme experiments, chrysin has shown activity against aromatase and a range of other targets [1][2]. Reviews of flavonoids note that absorption is the limiting factor: oral bioavailability is reported as roughly 0.003 to 0.02 percent, with rapid excretion [2]. A paper titled "No evidence for the in vivo activity of aromatase-inhibiting flavonoids" is cited in this context [2].
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports that, as of 2016, no toxicity had been attributed to chrysin in clinical trials or adverse event reports, while noting nonclinical data raising possible concerns; one review considers 0.5 to 3 g daily intake safe [2]. In 2016 the FDA did not recommend adding chrysin to the bulk-substances list for compounding [2].
